claim: Small arteries from mice with smooth muscle-specific loss of G12/G13 have lost myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: Here, we show that small arteries from mice with smooth muscle-specific loss of G12/G13 or the Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor ARHGEF12 have lost myogenic vasoconstriction.
evidence: Supported by pressure myography experiments showing complete loss of active vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 1B).

claim: Small arteries from mice with smooth muscle-specific loss of ARHGEF12 have lost myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: Here, we show that small arteries from mice with smooth muscle-specific loss of G12/G13 or the Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor ARHGEF12 have lost myogenic vasoconstriction.
evidence: Supported by pressure myography experiments showing loss of myogenic response in mesenteric arteries from Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 1H).

claim: The defect in myogenic vasoconstriction in G12/G13-deficient vessels was accompanied by loss of RhoA activation.
source: This defect was accompanied by loss of RhoA activation, while vessels showed normal increases in intracellular [Ca2+].
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assays showing strongly reduced RhoA activity in pressurized mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 1E).

claim: Vessels from G12/G13-deficient mice showed normal increases in intracellular [Ca2+] during myogenic tone development.
source: This defect was accompanied by loss of RhoA activation, while vessels showed normal increases in intracellular [Ca2+].
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging showing that intracellular Ca2+ increases were unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency (Figure 1I-K).

claim: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, perfusion of peripheral organs was increased.
source: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, perfusion of peripheral organs was increased, systemic vascular resistance was reduced and cardiac output and left ventricular mass were increased.
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging showing increased hindlimb and brain perfusion in Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 2B-D).

claim: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, systemic vascular resistance was reduced.
source: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, perfusion of peripheral organs was increased, systemic vascular resistance was reduced and cardiac output and left ventricular mass were increased.
evidence: Supported by kidney perfusion experiments showing reduced increase in renal vascular resistance in Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 2A) and increased cardiac output (Figure 3C).

claim: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, cardiac output was increased.
source: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, perfusion of peripheral organs was increased, systemic vascular resistance was reduced and cardiac output and left ventricular mass were increased.
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements showing significantly enhanced cardiac output in Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 3C).

claim: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, left ventricular mass was increased.
source: In the absence of myogenic vasoconstriction, perfusion of peripheral organs was increased, systemic vascular resistance was reduced and cardiac output and left ventricular mass were increased.
evidence: Supported by MRI data showing significantly increased left ventricular mass in Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Animals with defective myogenic vasoconstriction showed aggravated hypotension in response to endotoxin.
source: In addition, animals with defective myogenic vasoconstriction showed aggravated hypotension in response to endotoxin.
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements showing prolonged and significantly increased hypotension after LPS injection in Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 5).

claim: G12/G13- and Rho-mediated signaling plays a key role in myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: We conclude that G12/G13- and Rho-mediated signaling plays a key role in myogenic vasoconstriction and that myogenic tone is required to maintain local and systemic vascular resistance under physiological and pathological condition.
evidence: Supported by multiple experiments showing loss of myogenic response, reduced RhoA activation, and reduced MYPT1 phosphorylation in G12/G13-deficient vessels.

claim: Myogenic tone is required to maintain local and systemic vascular resistance under physiological and pathological conditions.
source: We conclude that G12/G13- and Rho-mediated signaling plays a key role in myogenic vasoconstriction and that myogenic tone is required to maintain local and systemic vascular resistance under physiological and pathological condition.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased organ perfusion, reduced vascular resistance, and aggravated LPS-induced hypotension in mice lacking myogenic tone.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction is an autoregulatory function of small arteries.
source: Myogenic vasoconstriction is an autoregulatory function of small arteries.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about myogenic vasoconstriction.

claim: Bayliss first described the myogenic response in 1902.
source: A particular form of autoregulation, the myogenic response, was first described by Bayliss (1902), who observed that stretch imposed on the vascular wall by an increase in intraluminal pressure induced a contraction of the vessel.
evidence: This is a historical citation referencing Bayliss's original work.

claim: Stretch imposed on the vascular wall by an increase in intraluminal pressure induces a contraction of the vessel.
source: A particular form of autoregulation, the myogenic response, was first described by Bayliss (1902), who observed that stretch imposed on the vascular wall by an increase in intraluminal pressure induced a contraction of the vessel.
evidence: This is a description of Bayliss's observation, supported by citation.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction has been observed in a variety of vascular beds.
source: This ability of vascular smooth muscle cells to respond to mechanical stretch has been observed in a variety of vascular beds.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the widespread occurrence of myogenic responses.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction is involved in maintaining basal vascular tone to promote constant perfusion despite fluctuations in perfusion pressure.
source: It has been suggested that myogenic vasoconstriction is involved in maintaining basal vascular tone to promote constant perfusion despite fluctuations in perfusion pressure and to prevent tissue damage in cases of overperfusion (Davis and Hill, 1999; Loutzenhiser et al., 2002; Walsh and Cole, 2013; Carlström et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction prevents tissue damage in cases of overperfusion.
source: It has been suggested that myogenic vasoconstriction is involved in maintaining basal vascular tone to promote constant perfusion despite fluctuations in perfusion pressure and to prevent tissue damage in cases of overperfusion (Davis and Hill, 1999; Loutzenhiser et al., 2002; Walsh and Cole, 2013; Carlström et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: In vivo evidence for the function of myogenic vasoconstriction is still lacking.
source: However, in vivo evidence for this is still lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The myogenic response goes along with phosphorylation of the myosin light chain (MLC).
source: As any vascular smooth muscle contraction, the myogenic response goes along with phosphorylation of the myosin light chain (MLC), which allows myosin to interact with actin and to generate contractile forces (Somlyo et al., 2004; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about smooth muscle contraction mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: MLC phosphorylation allows myosin to interact with actin and to generate contractile forces.
source: As any vascular smooth muscle contraction, the myogenic response goes along with phosphorylation of the myosin light chain (MLC), which allows myosin to interact with actin and to generate contractile forces (Somlyo et al., 2004; Vetterkind and Morgan, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about smooth muscle contraction mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: MLC phosphorylation can be increased by activation of the MLC kinase (MLCK) through a Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent mechanism.
source: MLC phosphorylation can be increased by activation of the MLC kinase (MLCK) through a Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent mechanism or by inhibition of myosin phosphatase via the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Somlyo and Somlyo, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MLC phosphorylation regulation, supported by citation.

claim: MLC phosphorylation can be increased by inhibition of myosin phosphatase via the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway.
source: MLC phosphorylation can be increased by activation of the MLC kinase (MLCK) through a Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent mechanism or by inhibition of myosin phosphatase via the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Somlyo and Somlyo, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MLC phosphorylation regulation, supported by citation.

claim: Both stretch-activated ion channels and mechanically activated G-protein-coupled receptors have been shown to play a role in the initiation of the myogenic response.
source: Both stretch-activated ion channels and mechanically activated G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) have been shown to play a role in the initiation of the myogenic response (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Schubert et al., 2008; Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Induction of vascular myogenic contraction requires membrane depolarization through activation of mechanically activated ion channels.
source: It is widely believed that induction of vascular myogenic contraction requires membrane depolarization through activation of mechanically activated ion channels which would then induce opening of voltage-dependent calcium channels resulting in an increase in intracellular calcium concentration (Davis and Hill, 1999; Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Knot and Nelson, 1998; Welsh et al., 2002; Jensen et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Membrane depolarization induces opening of voltage-dependent calcium channels resulting in an increase in intracellular calcium concentration.
source: It is widely believed that induction of vascular myogenic contraction requires membrane depolarization through activation of mechanically activated ion channels which would then induce opening of voltage-dependent calcium channels resulting in an increase in intracellular calcium concentration (Davis and Hill, 1999; Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Knot and Nelson, 1998; Welsh et al., 2002; Jensen et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several ion channels have been involved in stretch-induced depolarization, including TRPC6 and TRPM4.
source: Although several ion channels have been involved in stretch-induced depolarization, including the transient receptor potential (TRP) channels TRPC6 and TRPM4, the molecular nature of the channel responsible for stretch-induced depolarization of vascular smooth muscle cells has remained elusive (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The molecular nature of the channel responsible for stretch-induced depolarization of vascular smooth muscle cells has remained elusive.
source: Although several ion channels have been involved in stretch-induced depolarization, including the transient receptor potential (TRP) channels TRPC6 and TRPM4, the molecular nature of the channel responsible for stretch-induced depolarization of vascular smooth muscle cells has remained elusive (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Several GPCRs have been involved in the myogenic response of vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: More recently, several GPCRs have been involved in the myogenic response of vascular smooth muscle cells (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of recent research findings, supported by citations.

claim: GPCRs involved in myogenic response include the purinergic P2Y6 receptor, the thromboxane A2 (TP) receptor, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors, the angiotensin AT1 receptor, and the cysteinyl leukotriene one receptors (CysLT1Rs).
source: These include the purinergic P2Y6 receptor, the thromboxane A2 (TP) receptor, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors as well as the angiotensin AT1 receptor and the cysteinyl leukotriene one receptors (CysLT1Rs) (Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2008; Schleifenbaum et al., 2014; Storch et al., 2015; Kauffenstein et al., 2016; Kroetsch and Bolz, 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Stretch-induced activation of P2Y6, TP and S1P receptors is believed to involve the release of agonistic ligands.
source: While stretch-induced activation of P2Y6, TP and S1P receptors is believed to involve the release of agonistic ligands (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Kauffenstein et al., 2016; Kroetsch and Bolz, 2013), evidence has been provided that mechanical activation of AT1 and CysLT1 receptors occurs in an agonist-independent manner (Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016; Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2008; Storch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Mechanical activation of AT1 and CysLT1 receptors occurs in an agonist-independent manner.
source: While stretch-induced activation of P2Y6, TP and S1P receptors is believed to involve the release of agonistic ligands (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Kauffenstein et al., 2016; Kroetsch and Bolz, 2013), evidence has been provided that mechanical activation of AT1 and CysLT1 receptors occurs in an agonist-independent manner (Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016; Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2008; Storch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: GPCRs implicated in vascular myogenic contraction can couple to several G-proteins including Gq/G11 and G12/G13.
source: The GPCRs implicated in vascular myogenic contraction can couple to several G-proteins including Gq/G11 and G12/G13 (Kauffenstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR signaling, supported by citation.

claim: Coupling of receptors to Gq/G11 through stimulation of phospholipase C-β results in the Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent activation of MLCK in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: Previous work has shown that in vascular smooth muscle cells coupling of receptors to Gq/G11 through stimulation of phospholipase C-β results in the Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent activation of MLCK, whereas coupling to G12/G13 via activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway results in the inhibition of myosin phosphatase and that these two pathways can synergize (Gohla et al., 2000; Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003; Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Coupling to G12/G13 via activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway results in the inhibition of myosin phosphatase in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: Previous work has shown that in vascular smooth muscle cells coupling of receptors to Gq/G11 through stimulation of phospholipase C-β results in the Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent activation of MLCK, whereas coupling to G12/G13 via activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway results in the inhibition of myosin phosphatase and that these two pathways can synergize (Gohla et al., 2000; Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003; Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The Gq/G11 and G12/G13 pathways can synergize in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: Previous work has shown that in vascular smooth muscle cells coupling of receptors to Gq/G11 through stimulation of phospholipase C-β results in the Ca2+- and calmodulin-dependent activation of MLCK, whereas coupling to G12/G13 via activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway results in the inhibition of myosin phosphatase and that these two pathways can synergize (Gohla et al., 2000; Somlyo and Somlyo, 2003; Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Myogenic contraction can be strongly reduced by pharmacological inhibition of Rho-kinase downstream of G12/G13.
source: Myogenic contraction can be strongly reduced by pharmacological inhibition of Rho-kinase downstream of G12/G13 (Schubert et al., 2008; Li and Brayden, 2017; Moreno-Domínguez et al., 2013; Schubert et al., 2002; Gokina et al., 2005) as well as of Gq/G11 (Storch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Myogenic contraction can be reduced by pharmacological inhibition of Gq/G11.
source: Myogenic contraction can be strongly reduced by pharmacological inhibition of Rho-kinase downstream of G12/G13 (Schubert et al., 2008; Li and Brayden, 2017; Moreno-Domínguez et al., 2013; Schubert et al., 2002; Gokina et al., 2005) as well as of Gq/G11 (Storch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Mesenteric arteries from Sm-q/11-KO mice showed comparable myogenic contraction to wild-type mice.
source: Mesenteric arteries from Sm-q/11-KO mice behaved like wild-type mice and showed comparable myogenic contraction (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data showing no significant difference in myogenic tone between control and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 1A).

claim: Mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice completely lacked active vasoconstriction indicating loss of myogenic contraction.
source: In contrast, mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice completely lacked active vasoconstriction indicating loss of myogenic contraction (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), a finding also made in third order mesenteric arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data showing complete loss of myogenic tone in Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 1B).

claim: Third order mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice lacked myogenic contraction.
source: In contrast, mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice completely lacked active vasoconstriction indicating loss of myogenic contraction (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), a finding also made in third order mesenteric arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data on third order mesenteric arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).

claim: Proximal cerebral arteries from Sm-q/11-KO mice showed myogenic response indistinguishable from wild-type mice.
source: When proximal cerebral arteries were exposed to stepwise increases in intraluminal pressure, an active vasoconstriction was observed in vessels of wild-type mice, which was indistinguishable from the response observed in vessels from mice with induced smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 deficiency (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data on cerebral arteries showing no significant difference between control and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 1C).

claim: The myogenic response in cerebral vessels from Sm-12/13-KO animals was significantly reduced.
source: However, the myogenic response in vessels from induced smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13-deficient animals was significantly reduced (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data on cerebral arteries showing significantly reduced myogenic tone in Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 1D).

claim: The myogenic response of cerebral vessels depends on a functional G12/G13-mediated signaling pathway.
source: Thus, similar to mesenteric vessels, the myogenic response of cerebral vessels does not require Gq/G11-mediated signaling in smooth muscle cells but depends on a functional G12/G13-mediated signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cerebral vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice showed reduced myogenic response while Sm-q/11-KO mice did not.

claim: The myogenic response of cerebral vessels does not require Gq/G11-mediated signaling in smooth muscle cells.
source: Thus, similar to mesenteric vessels, the myogenic response of cerebral vessels does not require Gq/G11-mediated signaling in smooth muscle cells but depends on a functional G12/G13-mediated signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cerebral vessels from Sm-q/11-KO mice showed normal myogenic response.

claim: In pressurized mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice, RhoA activity was strongly reduced compared to vessels from wild-type and Sm-q/11-KO mice.
source: In pressurized mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice, RhoA activity was strongly reduced compared to vessels from wild-type and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assays using G-LISA kit (Figure 1E).

claim: The Rho-kinase inhibitor Y-27632 blocked myogenic response in mesenteric arteries.
source: Consistent with published data (Gokina et al., 2005; Dubroca et al., 2005), we found that the Rho-kinase inhibitor Y-27632 blocked myogenic response in mesenteric arteries (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography experiments with Y-27632 treatment (Figure 1F).

claim: Phosphorylation of MYPT1 was increased in pressurized wild-type mesenteric arteries.
source: In addition, we found that phosphorylation of the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, MYPT1, a substrate of Rho-kinase, was increased in pressurized wild-type mesenteric arteries, but in vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice this effect could not be observed any more (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing increased P-MYPT1 in pressurized control arteries (Figure 1G).

claim: In vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice, phosphorylation of MYPT1 during pressurization could not be observed.
source: In addition, we found that phosphorylation of the regulatory subunit of myosin phosphatase, MYPT1, a substrate of Rho-kinase, was increased in pressurized wild-type mesenteric arteries, but in vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice this effect could not be observed any more (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing no increase in P-MYPT1 in pressurized Sm-12/13-KO arteries (Figure 1G).

claim: ARHGEF12 couples G12/G13 to the regulation of RhoA activity in vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: The Rho-guanine nucleotide exchange factor 12 (ARHGEF12, also known as leukemia-associated RhoGEF (LARG)) has been shown to couple G12/G13 to the regulation of RhoA activity in vascular smooth muscle cells (Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: In mesenteric arteries from Sm-Larg-KO mice, RhoA activation was decreased.
source: We therefore tested myogenic contraction in mesenteric arteries from tamoxifen-induced smooth muscle-specific ARHGEF12-deficient animals (Sm-Larg-KO) and found that, similar to vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice, RhoA activation was decreased (Figure 1E), and the myogenic response was abrogated (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RhoA activity assays showing decreased RhoA activity in Sm-Larg-KO vessels (Figure 1E).

claim: The myogenic response was abrogated in mesenteric arteries from Sm-Larg-KO mice.
source: We therefore tested myogenic contraction in mesenteric arteries from tamoxifen-induced smooth muscle-specific ARHGEF12-deficient animals (Sm-Larg-KO) and found that, similar to vessels from Sm-12/13-KO mice, RhoA activation was decreased (Figure 1E), and the myogenic response was abrogated (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data showing loss of myogenic tone in Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 1H).

claim: G12/G13-mediated Rho/Rho-kinase activation is required for myogenic contraction.
source: These data strongly indicate that G12/G13-mediated Rho/Rho-kinase activation is required for myogenic contraction.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing loss of myogenic response, reduced RhoA activation, and reduced MYPT1 phosphorylation in G12/G13-deficient vessels.

claim: An increase in intracellular [Ca2+] occurs during myogenic contraction.
source: To test whether the increase in intracellular [Ca2+] described to occur during myogenic contraction (Gokina et al., 2005; D'Angelo et al., 1997) was affected by smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 or Gα12/Gα13 deficiency, we loaded mesenteric arteries with Fura-2AM and determined the intracellular free Ca2+ concentration during the stepwise increases in intraluminal pressure (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: An increase in [Ca2+]i accompanied the myogenic response in vessels from wild-type mice.
source: We observed in vessels from wild-type mice an increase in [Ca2+]i, which accompanied the myogenic response.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging data (Figure 1I-K).

claim: The increase in [Ca2+]i during myogenic response was unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 deficiency.
source: However, this response was unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 and Gα12/Gα13 deficiency (Figure 1I–K), whereas inhibition of L-type Ca2+ channels and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels by nifedipine and 2-ABP, respectively, reduced the increase in [Ca2+]i by about 50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging data showing no difference between control and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 1I).

claim: The increase in [Ca2+]i during myogenic response was unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: However, this response was unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 and Gα12/Gα13 deficiency (Figure 1I–K), whereas inhibition of L-type Ca2+ channels and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels by nifedipine and 2-ABP, respectively, reduced the increase in [Ca2+]i by about 50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging data showing no difference between control and Sm-12/13-KO mice (Figure 1J).

claim: Inhibition of L-type Ca2+ channels and TRP channels by nifedipine and 2-ABP reduced the increase in [Ca2+]i by about 50%.
source: However, this response was unaffected by smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11 and Gα12/Gα13 deficiency (Figure 1I–K), whereas inhibition of L-type Ca2+ channels and transient receptor potential (TRP) channels by nifedipine and 2-ABP, respectively, reduced the increase in [Ca2+]i by about 50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging data with nifedipine and 2-ABP treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Kidneys from Sm-12/13-KO animals showed a significantly reduced increase in renal vascular resistance when perfused at increasing pressures.
source: When isolated kidneys were perfused at increasing pressures, an increase in the vascular resistance could be observed, which did not differ between kidneys from wild-type mice and kidneys from Sm-q/11-KO animals (Figure 2A). In contrast, kidneys from Sm-12/13-KO animals showed a significantly reduced increase in renal vascular resistance (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by isolated kidney perfusion experiments (Figure 2A).

claim: Kidneys from wild-type mice and Sm-q/11-KO animals showed similar increases in vascular resistance when perfused at increasing pressures.
source: When isolated kidneys were perfused at increasing pressures, an increase in the vascular resistance could be observed, which did not differ between kidneys from wild-type mice and kidneys from Sm-q/11-KO animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by isolated kidney perfusion experiments (Figure 2A).

claim: Sm-12/13-KO animals showed significantly increased hind limb perfusion after induction compared to control and Sm-q/11-KO mice.
source: To analyze the role of vascular smooth muscle G12/G13 and Gq/G11 in hindlimb perfusion, we determined perfusion before and after tamoxifen-induced recombination using laser speckle imaging. Sm-12/13-KO as well as Sm-Larg-KO animals showed significantly increased hind limb perfusion after induction compared to control and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging data (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Sm-Larg-KO animals showed significantly increased hind limb perfusion after induction compared to control and Sm-q/11-KO mice.
source: To analyze the role of vascular smooth muscle G12/G13 and Gq/G11 in hindlimb perfusion, we determined perfusion before and after tamoxifen-induced recombination using laser speckle imaging. Sm-12/13-KO as well as Sm-Larg-KO animals showed significantly increased hind limb perfusion after induction compared to control and Sm-q/11-KO mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging data (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Brains from Sm-12/13-KO animals showed an increased brain perfusion compared to wild-type and Sm-q/11-KO animals.
source: Consistent with the loss of myogenic contraction in proximal cerebral arteries of Sm-12/13-KO mice, semiquantitative laser speckle imaging of brains from Sm-12/13-KO animals showed an increased brain perfusion compared to wild-type and Sm-q/11-KO animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging data of brain perfusion (Figure 2D).

claim: Brains from Sm-Larg-KO animals showed increased brain perfusion.
source: This phenotype was also observed in Sm-Larg-KO animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging data of brain perfusion (Figure 2D).

claim: The G12/G13-mediated myogenic response is required for the autoregulation of vessels of the hind limb, kidney and brain.
source: These data show that the G12/G13-mediated myogenic response is required for the autoregulation of vessels of the hind limb, kidney and brain and suggests a reduced peripheral vascular resistance in these animals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased perfusion in multiple organs in Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice.

claim: Within a few weeks after induction of Sm-12/13 KO mice, no major dysfunction of the kidney or brain was observed.
source: Within a few weeks after induction of Sm-12/13 KO mice, we did not observe any major dysfunction of the kidney or brain in these animals when analyzing urine volume, glomerular filtration rate, blood urea nitrogen and plasma creatinine levels or after performing several tests for motoric functions and after analyzing circadian activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by kidney function tests and motor coordination tests showing no significant differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Both heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area of Sm-12/13-KO mice were significantly increased compared to wild-type animals.
source: Both heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area of Sm-12/13-KO mice were significantly increased compared to wild-type animals without any sign of fibrosis or change in capillary density (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and quantification (Figure 3A).

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice showed no sign of cardiac fibrosis.
source: Both heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area of Sm-12/13-KO mice were significantly increased compared to wild-type animals without any sign of fibrosis or change in capillary density (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis with picrosirius red staining (Figure 3A).

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice showed no change in capillary density.
source: Both heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area of Sm-12/13-KO mice were significantly increased compared to wild-type animals without any sign of fibrosis or change in capillary density (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis with IB4 staining (Figure 3A).

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice had a significantly increased left ventricular mass.
source: Using magnetic resonance imaging, we confirmed that Sm-12/13-KO mice had a significantly increased left ventricular mass (Figure 3B) and found that left ventricular ejection fraction, stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly enhanced, whereas the heart rate was not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements (Figure 3B).

claim: Left ventricular ejection fraction was significantly enhanced in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: Using magnetic resonance imaging, we confirmed that Sm-12/13-KO mice had a significantly increased left ventricular mass (Figure 3B) and found that left ventricular ejection fraction, stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly enhanced, whereas the heart rate was not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Stroke volume was significantly enhanced in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: Using magnetic resonance imaging, we confirmed that Sm-12/13-KO mice had a significantly increased left ventricular mass (Figure 3B) and found that left ventricular ejection fraction, stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly enhanced, whereas the heart rate was not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Heart rate was not affected in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: Using magnetic resonance imaging, we confirmed that Sm-12/13-KO mice had a significantly increased left ventricular mass (Figure 3B) and found that left ventricular ejection fraction, stroke volume and cardiac output were significantly enhanced, whereas the heart rate was not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Loss of smooth muscle Gα12/Gα13 expression had no effect on the blood pressure.
source: Loss of smooth muscle Gα12/Gα13 expression had no effect on the blood pressure as reported previously (Wirth et al., 2008) indicating a reduced peripheral vascular resistance in these animals.
evidence: This is a reference to previously published data, supported by citation.

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice have a reduced peripheral vascular resistance.
source: Loss of smooth muscle Gα12/Gα13 expression had no effect on the blood pressure as reported previously (Wirth et al., 2008) indicating a reduced peripheral vascular resistance in these animals.
evidence: Inferred from normal blood pressure combined with increased cardiac output.

claim: Expression of Acta1, Myh7, Nppa and Nppb was not increased 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: To analyze whether the myocardial hypertrophy in Sm-12/13-KO mice was accompanied by increased expression of fetal genes, which would indicate a pathological form of hypertrophy, we analyzed expression of Acta1, Myh7, Nppa and Nppb 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency. However, expression of none of these genes was increased (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4A).

claim: Nppa, Nppb and Acta1 showed a decreased expression 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: Nppa, Nppb and Acta1 rather showed a decreased expression.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4A).

claim: Expression of different fibrosis markers was unchanged 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: In addition, expression of different fibrosis markers was unchanged, and plasma catecholamine, angiotensin II and aldosterone levels were comparable between wild-type and Sm-12/13-KO mice 4 weeks after induction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4A).

claim: Plasma catecholamine, angiotensin II and aldosterone levels were comparable between wild-type and Sm-12/13-KO mice 4 weeks after induction.
source: In addition, expression of different fibrosis markers was unchanged, and plasma catecholamine, angiotensin II and aldosterone levels were comparable between wild-type and Sm-12/13-KO mice 4 weeks after induction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 4B).

claim: Hypertrophy marker genes were still unchanged or slightly reduced 35 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: Thirty five weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency, hypertrophy marker genes were still unchanged or slightly reduced, and plasma levels of catecholamines, angiotensin II and aldosterone were unchanged (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4C).

claim: Plasma levels of catecholamines, angiotensin II and aldosterone were unchanged 35 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: Thirty five weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency, hypertrophy marker genes were still unchanged or slightly reduced, and plasma levels of catecholamines, angiotensin II and aldosterone were unchanged (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 4D).

claim: Two of six fibrosis marker genes were upregulated by 50–100% 35 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: While 2 of the six fibrosis marker genes were upregulated by 50–100% (Figure 4C) 35 weeks after induction, sirius red staining showed no signs of fibrosis in hearts 35 weeks after induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4C).

claim: Sirius red staining showed no signs of fibrosis in hearts 35 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency.
source: While 2 of the six fibrosis marker genes were upregulated by 50–100% (Figure 4C) 35 weeks after induction, sirius red staining showed no signs of fibrosis in hearts 35 weeks after induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: LPS induced a transient decrease in arterial blood pressure by maximally 15 mmHg in wild-type animals.
source: While LPS induced a transient decrease in arterial blood pressure by maximally 15 mmHg in wild-type animals, the same dose of LPS resulted in a prolonged and significantly increased hypotension when given to Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements (Figure 5).

claim: The same dose of LPS resulted in a prolonged and significantly increased hypotension when given to Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice.
source: While LPS induced a transient decrease in arterial blood pressure by maximally 15 mmHg in wild-type animals, the same dose of LPS resulted in a prolonged and significantly increased hypotension when given to Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by telemetric blood pressure measurements (Figure 5).

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction requires smooth muscle cell depolarization and increases in the free intracellular Ca2+ concentration which involve opening of cation channels in the plasma membrane.
source: Small arteries are able to contract in response to increases in intravascular pressure. This myogenic vasoconstriction requires smooth muscle cell depolarization and increases in the free intracellular Ca2+ concentration which involve opening of cation channels in the plasma membrane (Tykocki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about myogenic vasoconstriction mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: GPCRs play a critical role in myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: However, multiple evidence has been provided that also GPCRs play a critical role in myogenic vasoconstriction (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Most vasocontractile receptors activate both the G12/G13-mediated pathway resulting in activation of RhoA and the Gq/G11-mediated pathway leading to phospholipase-β activation and IP3-dependent Ca2+ mobilization.
source: Most of these vasocontractile receptors have been shown to activate both the G12/G13-mediated pathway resulting in activation of RhoA as well as the Gq/G11-mediated pathway leading to phospholipase-β activation and IP3-dependent Ca2+ mobilization (Gohla et al., 2000; Wirth et al., 2008; Bolz et al., 2003; Sauzeau et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: GPCR signaling through both pathways increases MLC phosphorylation and contraction by activation of MLCK through a Ca2+-dependent pathway and by inhibition of myosin phosphatase through the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway.
source: This suggests that GPCR signaling through both pathways increases MLC phosphorylation and contraction by activation of MLCK through a Ca2+-dependent pathway and by inhibition of myosin phosphatase through the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Somlyo and Somlyo, 2000; Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction depends on G12/G13-mediated signaling but not on Gq/G11.
source: Based on the analysis of mesenteric and cerebral arteries from smooth muscle-specific Gαq/Gα11- and Gα12/Gα13-deficient mice, our data, however, indicate that myogenic vasoconstriction depends on G12/G13-mediated signaling but not on Gq/G11.
evidence: Supported by pressure myography experiments showing loss of myogenic response in Sm-12/13-KO but not Sm-q/11-KO mice.

claim: Rho/Rho-kinase-mediated signaling plays an important role in myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: This is supported by studies in vessels lacking the G12/G13-regulated Rho-GEF protein ARHGEF12 and is consistent with data showing that Rho/Rho-kinase-mediated signaling plays an important role in myogenic vasoconstriction (Schubert et al., 2008; de Godoy and Rattan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by data from Sm-Larg-KO mice and previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: A pharmacological Gαq/Gα11 inhibitor inhibits myogenic tone in 3rd order mesenteric arteries by about 65%.
source: In contrast to our data, it has been reported that a pharmacological Gαq/Gα11 inhibitor inhibits myogenic tone in 3rd order mesenteric arteries by about 65% (Mederos Y Schnitzler et al., 2016; Storch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings that contrast with the current study, supported by citations.

claim: The increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration during myogenic tone development was neither affected by smooth muscle-specific Gq/G11 deficiency nor by G12/G13 and LARG deficiency.
source: Our observation that the increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration during myogenic tone development was neither affected by smooth muscle-specific Gq/G11 deficiency nor by G12/G13 and LARG deficiency indicates that the Ca2+-dependent contraction during myogenic tone is not mediated by GPCRs.
evidence: Supported by Fura-2AM calcium imaging data (Figure 1I-K).

claim: The Ca2+-dependent contraction during myogenic tone is not mediated by GPCRs.
source: Our observation that the increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration during myogenic tone development was neither affected by smooth muscle-specific Gq/G11 deficiency nor by G12/G13 and LARG deficiency indicates that the Ca2+-dependent contraction during myogenic tone is not mediated by GPCRs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ca2+ increases were unaffected by loss of Gq/G11 or G12/G13.

claim: TRPC6 and TRPM4 have been reported to be activated through Gq/G11-mediated signaling induced by angiotensin-II and other receptors.
source: While TRPC6 and TRPM4 have been reported to be activated through Gq/G11-mediated signaling induced by angiotensin-II and other receptors (Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2008; Inoue et al., 2009; Pires et al., 2017), another report failed to observe Gq/G11-mediated enhancement of mechanically induced TRPC currents during myogenic vasoconstriction (Anfinogenova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of conflicting previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: A report failed to observe Gq/G11-mediated enhancement of mechanically induced TRPC currents during myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: While TRPC6 and TRPM4 have been reported to be activated through Gq/G11-mediated signaling induced by angiotensin-II and other receptors (Mederos y Schnitzler et al., 2008; Inoue et al., 2009; Pires et al., 2017), another report failed to observe Gq/G11-mediated enhancement of mechanically induced TRPC currents during myogenic vasoconstriction (Anfinogenova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: A recent study suggested that TRPM4 channel opening is promoted by the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway.
source: A recent study also suggested that TRPM4 channel opening is promoted by the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Li and Brayden, 2017) whereas other studies had found no involvement of this pathway in TRP channel regulation during myogenic tone development (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Other studies had found no involvement of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway in TRP channel regulation during myogenic tone development.
source: A recent study also suggested that TRPM4 channel opening is promoted by the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Li and Brayden, 2017) whereas other studies had found no involvement of this pathway in TRP channel regulation during myogenic tone development (Kauffenstein et al., 2012; Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: Gq/G11-mediated signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells does not critically contribute to increases in intracellular free Ca2+ during myogenic tone development.
source: Our data indicate that Gq/G11-mediated signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells does not critically contribute to increases in intracellular free Ca2+ or smooth muscle contraction during myogenic tone development whereas the role of G12/G13-mediated signaling and its downstream RhoA-dependent signaling pathway is important for myogenic tone development but does not contribute to mechanically induced increases in intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing no effect of Gq/G11 deficiency on Ca2+ increases.

claim: Gq/G11-mediated signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells does not critically contribute to smooth muscle contraction during myogenic tone development.
source: Our data indicate that Gq/G11-mediated signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells does not critically contribute to increases in intracellular free Ca2+ or smooth muscle contraction during myogenic tone development whereas the role of G12/G13-mediated signaling and its downstream RhoA-dependent signaling pathway is important for myogenic tone development but does not contribute to mechanically induced increases in intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data showing no effect of Gq/G11 deficiency on myogenic tone.

claim: G12/G13-mediated signaling and its downstream RhoA-dependent signaling pathway is important for myogenic tone development but does not contribute to mechanically induced increases in intracellular Ca2+.
source: Our data indicate that Gq/G11-mediated signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells does not critically contribute to increases in intracellular free Ca2+ or smooth muscle contraction during myogenic tone development whereas the role of G12/G13-mediated signaling and its downstream RhoA-dependent signaling pathway is important for myogenic tone development but does not contribute to mechanically induced increases in intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of myogenic tone but normal Ca2+ increases in G12/G13-deficient vessels.

claim: Ca2+ influx through mechanically activated plasma membrane ion channels is primarily responsible for inducing Ca2+-dependent MLC phosphorylation during myogenic contraction.
source: These data are consistent with a model of dual regulation of MLC-phosphorylation during myogenic contraction through a Ca2+-dependent and a Rho/Rho-kinase-dependent pathway, in which Ca2+ influx through mechanically activated plasma membrane ion channels is primarily responsible for inducing Ca2+-dependent MLC phosphorylation, whereas activation of GPCRs via G12/G13 leads to activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and supported by Figure 6.

claim: Activation of GPCRs via G12/G13 leads to activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway during myogenic contraction.
source: These data are consistent with a model of dual regulation of MLC-phosphorylation during myogenic contraction through a Ca2+-dependent and a Rho/Rho-kinase-dependent pathway, in which Ca2+ influx through mechanically activated plasma membrane ion channels is primarily responsible for inducing Ca2+-dependent MLC phosphorylation, whereas activation of GPCRs via G12/G13 leads to activation of the Rho/Rho-kinase pathway (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and supported by Figure 6.

claim: The relevance of the Ca2+-dependent and Rho/Rho-kinase-dependent pathways may differ between different vascular beds.
source: It is possible that the relevance of these two pathways differs between different vascular beds.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of different degrees of myogenic response loss in different vascular beds.

claim: The myogenic response in cerebral arteries was reduced by about 50% in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: While we observed a complete loss of myogenic vasoconstriction in mesenteric arteries from Sm-12/13-KO mice, the myogenic response in cerebral arteries was not lost but reduced by about 50%.
evidence: Supported by pressure myography data on cerebral arteries (Figure 1D).

claim: Pressure-induced depolarization and Ca2+ signaling may play a more dominant role in cerebral arteries.
source: This may be due to a more dominant role of pressure-induced depolarization and Ca2+ signaling in cerebral arteries.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the difference in myogenic response loss between mesenteric and cerebral arteries.

claim: Gq/G11-mediated signaling downstream of GPCRs may contribute to Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent signaling but is not required for myogenic vasoconstriction.
source: Gq/G11-mediated signaling downstream of GPCRs may contribute to Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent signaling but is not required for myogenic vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Gq/G11 deficiency did not affect myogenic tone.

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice have a normal basal blood pressure.
source: Early observations showed that Sm-12/13-KO mice have a normal basal blood pressure but do not respond with arterial hypertension to desoxycorticosterone (DOCA)/NaCl treatment (Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice do not respond with arterial hypertension to desoxycorticosterone (DOCA)/NaCl treatment.
source: Early observations showed that Sm-12/13-KO mice have a normal basal blood pressure but do not respond with arterial hypertension to desoxycorticosterone (DOCA)/NaCl treatment (Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Sm-12/13-KO mice have an increased cardiac output due to an increased stroke volume.
source: The present study indicates that Sm-12/13-KO mice have an increased cardiac output due to an increased stroke volume, suggesting that loss of myogenic tone in Sm-12/13-KO mice results in a reduced vascular resistance compensated by increased cardiac output.
evidence: Supported by MRI measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: Loss of myogenic tone in Sm-12/13-KO mice results in a reduced vascular resistance compensated by increased cardiac output.
source: The present study indicates that Sm-12/13-KO mice have an increased cardiac output due to an increased stroke volume, suggesting that loss of myogenic tone in Sm-12/13-KO mice results in a reduced vascular resistance compensated by increased cardiac output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased cardiac output and normal blood pressure.

claim: No signs of increased sympathetic activity were found in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: Interestingly, we did not find signs of increased sympathetic activity or changes in angiotensin II and aldosterone levels.
evidence: Supported by catecholamine measurements (Figure 4B and D).

claim: No changes in angiotensin II and aldosterone levels were found in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
source: Interestingly, we did not find signs of increased sympathetic activity or changes in angiotensin II and aldosterone levels.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 4B and D).

claim: The increased stroke volume and increased cardiac output might be the result of a reduced afterload.
source: Thus, the increased stroke volume and increased cardiac output might just be the result of a reduced afterload.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased cardiac output without increased sympathetic activity.

claim: Similar observations have been made during physical exercise or after pharmacological inhibition of peripheral resistance.
source: Similar observations have been made during physical exercise or after pharmacological inhibition of peripheral resistance (Andersen and Vik-Mo, 1984; Radovits et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The increased cardiac output was accompanied by myocardial hypertrophy resembling other forms of physiological hypertrophy.
source: The increased cardiac output was accompanied by myocardial hypertrophy resembling other forms of physiological hypertrophy as it did not go along with the expression of fetal genes such as those encoding natriuretic peptide A and B as well as the cardiac myosin heavy chain (Myh7) or skeletal muscle α-actin (Acta1) (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no increase in fetal gene expression (Figure 4A and C).

claim: Acta1 expression was reduced 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency, typical for physiological cardiac hypertrophy.
source: As described before, Acta1 expression was rather reduced 4 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency typical for physiological cardiac hypertrophy (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; McMullen and Jennings, 2007).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4A) and citations.

claim: The reduced peripheral resistance in Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice resulted in increased perfusion of the brain or the hind limb under basal conditions.
source: Our data clearly show that the reduced peripheral resistance in Sm-12/13-KO and Sm-Larg-KO mice resulting in increased cardiac output was accompanied by increased perfusion of the brain or the hind limb under basal conditions.
evidence: Supported by laser speckle imaging data (Figure 2B-D).

claim: G12/G13-mediated myogenic tone protects organs against overperfusion.
source: This indicates that G12/G13-mediated myogenic tone protects organs against overperfusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased organ perfusion in mice lacking myogenic tone.

claim: Even 34 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency and loss of myogenic tone, no obvious morphological or functional defects were observed in organs other than the heart.
source: However, even 34 weeks after induction of smooth muscle-specific Gα12/Gα13 deficiency and loss of myogenic tone, we did not observe any obvious morphological or functional defects in other organs than the heart.
evidence: This is a statement based on the absence of observed defects in kidney and brain function tests.

claim: No formation of edema was observed in mice lacking myogenic tone.
source: No formation of edema was observed as would have been expected from a loss of myogenic tone.
evidence: This is a statement based on the absence of observed edema.

claim: Myogenic vasoconstriction primarily functions to establish an underlying vascular tone on which humoral or neural vasodilatory and vasocontractile stimuli act to control the vascular diameter.
source: This indicates that the myogenic vasoconstriction primarily functions to establish an underlying vascular tone on which humoral or neural vasodilatory and vasocontractile stimuli act to control the vascular diameter and to also compensate to some degree alterations of myogenic tone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mice lacking myogenic tone do not show major organ dysfunction under basal conditions.

claim: Under pathological conditions when modulatory stimuli are dysregulated, myogenic autoregulation can only partially compensate the activity of vasoactive mediators.
source: However, under pathological conditions when these modulatory stimuli are dysregulated such as in severe cases of hypertension or hypotension myogenic autoregulation can only partially compensate the activity of vasoactive mediators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of aggravated hypotension in response to LPS in mice lacking myogenic tone.

claim: Loss of smooth muscle G12/G13-mediated signaling had no effect on basal blood pressure but strongly suppressed mineralocorticoid hypertension in the DOCA/salt model.
source: This is also indicated by earlier observations that loss of smooth muscle G12/G13-mediated signaling had no effect on basal blood pressure but strongly suppressed mineralocorticoid hypertension in the deoxycorticosterone/salt (DOCA/salt) model (Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research findings, supported by citation.

claim: Under septic conditions, G12/G13-mediated myogenic tone is still intact and provides partial resistance against vasodilatory influences.
source: Similarly, in the present study we show that endotoxin-induced hypotension is aggravated in Sm-12/13-KO mice suggesting that under septic conditions, which result in strong vasodilatation and hypotension, G12/G13-mediated myogenic tone is still intact and provides partial resistance against vasodilatory influences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of aggravated LPS-induced hypotension in Sm-12/13-KO mice.
